## Synthesis: research report

**Question:** Has anyone implemented cross-context KV cache splicing — reusing a precomputed key/value cache chunk at a NEW position in a different context — specifically via (1) RoPE re-anchoring / position-shifting of cached keys and (2) CacheBlend-style selective recomputation of a subset of tokens to heal cross-attention? I need concrete IMPLEMENTATIONS and HOW they did it, not just papers. Focus areas: (a) Does llama.cpp / ggml already expose a KV-cache position-shift or RoPE-shift operation (e.g. llama_kv_cache_seq_shift, llama_kv_self_seq_add/div, seq_rm, "context shifting", "self-extend", StreamingLLM support)? What is the actual API/op and how does it manipulate the raw K tensors in the cache? (b) Are there open-source implementations of CacheBlend (the EuroSys 2025 selective-recompute KV blending method) — e.g. in LMCache, vLLM, or the authors' own repo — and how do they perform the partial recompute and choose which tokens to heal? (c) Position-independent KV cache reuse implementations: EPIC, PromptCache, CacheClip, RedKnot, QCFuse, KVLink, block-attention — which have public code and what mechanism do they use to make a chunk's KV valid at an arbitrary position? (d) Any llama.cpp-specific or GGUF-specific attempts (issues, PRs, forks) at reusing/splicing KV computed in a different context. For each implementation found, report: the exact mechanism (RoPE rotation math, which tensors are touched, how healing/recompute is scoped), whether it's merged/maintained, what engine it targets, and any reported correctness or speed results. The goal is to learn from existing implementations before building a native ggml RoPE-shift + selective-heal kernel in a llama.cpp fork.

20 claims survived 3-vote adversarial verification. Merge semantic duplicates and synthesize.

## Confirmed claims
### [0] llama.cpp merged a port of Self-Extend (grouped-attention context extension) into the HTTP server in PR #5104, making runtime position/RoPE manipulation of the KV cache a maintained upstream feature.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/5104 (primary)
Quote: "Pull Request #5104 was **merged on January 27, 2024** by ggerganov into the master branch of ggml-org/llama.cpp."
Verifier evidence (high): PR #5104 "Port of self extension to server" was merged by ggerganov on Jan 27, 2024. Contributor Maximilian-Winter ported self-extend (grouped attention) into the llama.cpp HTTP server, adding --grp-attn-n / --grp-attn-w flags, mirroring the main-binary capability. Self-Extend is a grouped-attention context-extension method that manipulates token positions (runtime RoPE/position handling of the KV cache), so the claim's characterization is correct. It is in upstream master. Minor caveat: Self-Extend does position grouping at attention time rather than being a pure standalone KV-shift op like llama_kv_cache_seq_add, but the claim only asserts "runtime position/RoPE manipulation... upstream feature," which holds.

### [1] Self-Extend in llama.cpp is driven by two runtime parameters, --grp-attn-n (group factor G) and --grp-attn-w (window W), that reshape token positions to fit within the model's trained context, demonstrating an existing position-remapping mechanism over cached tokens.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/5104 (primary)
Quote: "Both parameters must satisfy: G ≥ (desired_context / training_context) and G must be a multiple of W"
Verifier evidence (high): Verified against llama.cpp PR #5104 ("Port of self extension to server") and server docs. Self-Extend in llama.cpp is genuinely controlled by two runtime params: --grp-attn-n (group attention factor G, default 1=disabled) and --grp-attn-w (group attention width W, default 512), exposing the SelfExtend paper's group-size and neighbor-window hyperparameters. These do reshape/remap token positions (grouped floor-division of positions) to keep them within the model's trained context, per LongLM Self-Extend (arXiv 2401.01325), extended length = (L - w)*G + w. llama.cpp enforces a divisibility constraint between grp-attn-n and grp-attn-w (n must be a multiple of w), matching the supporting quote. It is a real, existing position-remapping mechanism. Minor caveat: Self-Extend remaps positions of all tokens in the window during attention (a position-mapping trick), not literally a splice of a foreign precomputed KV chunk — but the claim only asserts a position-remapping mechanism exists, which is true. Primary source (merged PR + paper) is sufficient quality.

### [2] CacheBlend, as productized in LMCache, enables KV cache reuse at non-prefix positions by selectively recomputing a subset of tokens to heal cross-attention.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://docs.lmcache.ai/kv_cache_optimizations/blending.html (primary)
Quote: "CacheBlend enables KV cache reuse for non-prefix positions by recomputing a subset of tokens at non-prefix positions."
Verifier evidence (high): Claim is accurately supported by the quote and corroborated by multiple sources. Primary: LMCache official docs (docs.lmcache.ai/kv_cache_optimizations/blending.html) state verbatim "CacheBlend enables KV cache reuse for non-prefix positions by recomputing a subset of tokens at non-prefix positions." Corroborated by the peer-reviewed EuroSys'25 Best Paper "CacheBlend: Fast LLM Serving for RAG with Cached Knowledge Fusion" (arXiv 2405.16444; ACM TOCS 10.1145/3790254), which specifies the concrete healing mechanism: fully recompute layer 1, partially recompute layer 2, then select top-k tokens with largest V-matrix discrepancy for recomputation. CacheBlend is a real, integrated component of LMCache (open-source), not vaporware. Reported ~3x TTFT reduction / 100% RAG hit rate. Current (2025), primary-sourced, mechanism matches the claim exactly.

### [3] The fraction of tokens recomputed (healed) is a configurable ratio, exposed via LMCACHE_BLEND_RECOMPUTE_RATIOS with an example value of 0.15 (15%).
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://docs.lmcache.ai/kv_cache_optimizations/blending.html (primary)
Quote: "LMCACHE_BLEND_RECOMPUTE_RATIOS: Sets the proportion of tokens to recalculate (example: 0.15 or 15%)"
Verifier evidence (high): The primary source (docs.lmcache.ai blending page) directly confirms the claim. It documents the env var LMCACHE_BLEND_RECOMPUTE_RATIOS as "Ratio of tokens to recompute" with the example `os.environ["LMCACHE_BLEND_RECOMPUTE_RATIOS"] = "0.15"`, i.e. 15% of tokens recomputed. This matches the claim's wording (configurable ratio, exposed via that env var, example 0.15/15%) exactly. Source is the official LMCache docs — appropriate primary source for a config-detail claim. Not extraordinary, not outdated, not marketing. The only minor nuance is the var name is plural ("RATIOS"), consistent with LMCache/CacheBlend supporting per-layer or per-source lists, but the scalar 0.15 example is genuinely shown, so the claim is not an overreach.

### [4] Which tokens get recomputed is decided using a specific check layer (e.g. layer 1), configured via LMCACHE_BLEND_CHECK_LAYERS.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://docs.lmcache.ai/kv_cache_optimizations/blending.html (primary)
Quote: "LMCACHE_BLEND_CHECK_LAYERS: Specifies which layers determine token recomputation (example: layer 1)"
Verifier evidence (high): Primary source (LMCache docs, blending.html) directly supports the claim: LMCACHE_BLEND_CHECK_LAYERS "specifies which layers determine token recomputation" with the config example setting it to layer 1. This is consistent with CacheBlend's published method, where token selection for selective recompute is driven by attention deviation measured at a specific check layer. The claim ("which tokens get recomputed is decided using a specific check layer, e.g. layer 1, configured via LMCACHE_BLEND_CHECK_LAYERS") is an accurate restatement, not an overreach. Source is the official LMCache documentation — appropriate quality for this implementation-detail claim, and current (LMCache is actively maintained).

### [5] LMCache implements CacheBlend to extend KV reuse beyond prefix caching by reusing cached KV blocks at ANY position in the prompt (position-independent reuse), using selective token recomputation for quality recovery.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache (primary)
Quote: "extending "KV reuse beyond prefix caching by reusing cached KV blocks at any position in the prompt. This leverages CacheBlend to selectively recompute tokens for quality recovery.""
Verifier evidence (high): LMCache's official README and docs (docs.lmcache.ai/kv_cache_optimizations/blending.html) directly state: "Non-prefix KV reuse: Extend KV reuse beyond prefix caching by reusing cached KV blocks at any position in the prompt. This leverages CacheBlend to selectively recompute tokens for quality recovery." Docs further describe position-independent KV cache reuse requiring recomputation of a subset of tokens. CacheBlend is the EuroSys 2025 method; LMCache is its maintained integration (also into vLLM). The blog reports up to 4.5x TTFT speedup with ~15% recomputation on non-prefix caches. The claim matches the primary source verbatim in mechanism and scope — no overreach, current, high-quality primary source.

### [6] LMCache is the maintained open-source home of CacheBlend, targeting mainstream open-source serving engines, specifically vLLM (including vLLM V1 and multimodal models).
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache (primary)
Quote: "extends its turbo-boost to multimodal models in vLLM V1 ... integrated with mainstream open-source serving engines"
Verifier evidence (high): LMCache's official docs host a dedicated "Blending" page (docs.lmcache.ai/kv_cache_optimizations/blending.html) documenting CacheBlend, which reuses KV even when the prompt is not a prefix (RAG doc-swap) and blends multiple KV caches to preserve cross-attention. Search results confirm CacheBlend is now compatible with vLLM V1 HMA with dual-RoPE for SWA models and extends turbo-boost to multimodal models in vLLM V1. The repo has active releases and example files (kv_cache_sharing_lmcache_v1.py) targeting vLLM V1. CacheBlend's authors (U. Chicago, Kuntai Du et al.) are the LMCache team, making LMCache its maintained home. Claim targets vLLM specifically, which matches LMCache's stated integration focus.

### [7] CacheBlend enables reuse of precomputed KV caches at non-prefix positions by selectively recomputing the KV values of a small subset of tokens to partially update each reused cache, healing cross-attention.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.16444 (primary)
Quote: "selectively recomputes the KV values of a small subset of tokens to partially update each reused KV cache"
Verifier evidence (high): Claim is verbatim-supported by the primary source. CacheBlend abstract (arxiv 2405.16444, also ACM TOCS 10.1145/3790254): "reuses the precomputed KV caches, regardless prefix or not, and selectively recomputes the KV values of a small subset of tokens to partially update each reused KV cache." Purpose is exactly to handle non-prefix reuse where chunks ignore cross-attention with preceding text (RAG). Mechanism confirmed: full first-layer recompute, second-layer V-value comparison to select top-k discrepant tokens for healing. Peer-reviewed (EuroSys 2025 / ACM TOCS), primary and current. No contradicting source found; supporting works (CacheClip 2510.10129) cite it as the reference method.

### [8] CacheBlend reuses precomputed KV caches regardless of whether the chunk is at a prefix position, i.e. supports position-independent reuse.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.16444 (primary)
Quote: "reuses the precomputed KV caches, regardless prefix or not"
Verifier evidence (high): CacheBlend (arxiv 2405.16444, EuroSys 2025) explicitly claims and implements position-independent KV reuse. The paper's own framing: reused chunks "are not always the input prefix," making precomputed KV caches "not directly usable since they ignore cross-attention with the preceding texts," and CacheBlend "fuses multiple pre-computed KV caches, regardless of prefix or not, by selectively recomputing the KV cache of a small fraction of tokens." This exactly matches the claim. The quote is not an overreach — non-prefix reuse is the paper's entire raison d'être (vs. prefix-only reuse like PagedAttention/prefix caching). Source is the primary paper (arxiv abs/pdf, v3), and it is backed by a public implementation in LMCache (github, e.g. ForceInjection/AI-fundermentals cache_blend.md documents the LMCache integration). No credible source disputes this; it is a well-known, current (2025) result. Note: reuse is enabled by selective recompute to heal cross-attention, not by making the raw cached KV magically valid at arbitrary positions with zero cost — but the claim as worded ("supports position-independent reuse") is correct.

### [9] CacheBlend has an open-source implementation available in the LMCache project.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.16444 (primary)
Quote: "The code is available at: https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache"
Verifier evidence (high): LMCache's official blog (blog.lmcache.ai, 2025-03-31) states CacheBlend "is now released as part of the LMCache and vLLM Production Stack packages," confirming an open-source implementation in the LMCache repo (github.com/LMCache/LMCache). This matches the paper's supporting quote pointing to the same repo. CacheBlend won ACM EuroSys 2025 Best Paper; the LMCache implementation selectively recomputes a small subset of tokens to heal cross-attention when reusing KV at arbitrary positions (TTFT 2.2-3.3x, throughput 2.8-5x). Corroborated by LMCache docs, ACM DL, and 2026 third-party reviews. Claim is current and primary-sourced.

### [10] CacheClip is a CacheBlend-style selective KV-cache recomputation method: it precomputes per-chunk KV independently and heals cross-chunk attention by recomputing a selected subset of tokens, rather than using RoPE position-shifting/re-anchoring.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.10129 (primary)
Quote: "CacheClip integrates four techniques: (1) auxiliary-model-guided token selection for selective KV cache recomputation, (2) shared prefixes to eliminate redundant attention sinks, (3) a sliding-window grouping strategy to maintain local coherence during partial KV cache updates"
Verifier evidence (high): Primary source arxiv 2510.10129 (CacheClip: Accelerating RAG with Effective KV Cache Reuse) directly confirms the claim. It "integrates four techniques: (1) auxiliary-model-guided token selection for selective KV cache recomputation, (2) shared prefixes to eliminate redundant attention sinks, (3) a sliding-window grouping strategy... (4) CPU-GPU hybrid design." The paper's stated insight is that small auxiliary LLMs share last-layer attention distributions with the primary model, "enabling efficient identification of tokens critical for restoring inter-chunk attention" — i.e. it precomputes per-chunk KV independently and heals cross-chunk attention by recomputing a selected subset of tokens. This is explicitly a CacheBlend-lineage selective-recompute approach (adjustable recomputation ratio), NOT RoPE position-shifting/re-anchoring — no rotation math is used. The characterization ("CacheBlend-style selective recompute, not RoPE re-anchoring") is accurate. Source is the primary arXiv paper, recent (Oct 2025), matching claim strength.

### [11] CacheClip selects which tokens to recompute/heal by using a small auxiliary LLM whose last-layer attention distribution approximates the primary model's, identifying tokens critical for restoring inter-chunk attention.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.10129 (primary)
Quote: "small auxiliary LLMs exhibit similar last-layer attention distributions to primary LLMs (the target model for generation), enabling efficient identification of tokens critical for restoring inter-chunk attention"
Verifier evidence (high): The claim faithfully paraphrases the primary source. CacheClip's abstract (arxiv.org/abs/2510.10129) states its core insight verbatim: "small auxiliary LLMs exhibit similar last-layer attention distributions to primary LLMs (the target model for generation), enabling efficient identification of tokens critical for restoring inter-chunk attention." The paper lists as technique #1 "auxiliary-model-guided token selection for selective KV cache recomputation, where the auxiliary model is finetuned to improve selection accuracy." This matches the claim exactly: a small auxiliary LLM whose last-layer attention approximates the primary model selects which tokens to recompute/heal. No contradicting source found; the claim is not an overreach. One minor nuance: the auxiliary model is finetuned to improve selection accuracy (claim omits this but does not contradict it). Source is the primary paper itself (Oct 2025), current for a fast-moving field, quality appropriate to the descriptive claim.

### [12] KVLink decouples RoPE from stored KV states by caching pre-rotation key states (W_k*x) and reapplying global rotary embeddings at each token's correct full-sequence position at inference time, so a chunk's KV becomes valid at a new position.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2502.16002v2 (primary)
Quote: "we decouple the key-value states from the positional embeddings when storing them ... apply the global rotary embedding for the KV states of each token appropriate to its location in the full sequence."
Verifier evidence (high): Primary source arxiv 2502.16002v2 directly confirms the claim. It states KVLink "decouple[s] the key-value states from the positional embeddings when storing them, i.e., W{k,v}·x_i" (pre-rotation states, excluding the RoPE rotation matrix R_i), and at inference "apply[s] the global rotary embedding for the KV states of each token appropriate to its location in the full sequence." This is exactly the mechanism claimed: cache pre-RoPE key states, reapply global rotary at correct full-sequence positions so a chunk's KV is valid at a new position. Minor imprecision: RoPE rotates only keys, not values, so "reapplying rotary to KV" is loosely worded — but this mirrors the paper's own wording and does not falsify the claim. Note KVLink's full method also adds trained 'link' tokens to heal cross-attention; the RoPE-decoupling sub-claim is accurate on its own. Source is the primary paper (v2), current (2025), matching claim strength.

### [13] Instead of recomputing a subset of document tokens, KVLink inserts a small set of trainable 'link tokens' between independently encoded segments whose KV is computed at inference to heal cross-segment attention.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2502.16002v2 (primary)
Quote: "we append a small set of trainable tokens between each segment's precomputed KV states before concatenation. The KV representations for these tokens are computed during inference."
Verifier evidence (high): Claim is directly supported by the arXiv 2502.16002v2 quote and corroborated by search summaries. KVLink "appends a small set of trainable tokens between each segment's precomputed KV states before concatenation," and "the KV representations for these tokens are computed during inference." These cross-segment link tokens attend to preceding tokens to restore self/cross-attention across independently encoded segments. The claim accurately paraphrases this without overreach. Minor caveat: KVLink also fine-tunes the model and re-adjusts positional embeddings to global positions — the link tokens are one of several components, not the sole healing mechanism — but the specific claim about link tokens is faithful. Source is the primary paper (NeurIPS 2025 poster), current (2025), not marketing.

### [14] EPIC enables position-independent KV cache reuse (PIC), allowing KV vectors of a text chunk to be reused regardless of the preceding prefix/position, rather than recomputing prefill for every new context.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://openreview.net/forum?id=qjd3ZUiHRT (primary)
Quote: "The paper introduces Position-Independent Caching (PIC) to enable KV vector reuse regardless of prefix variations."
Verifier evidence (high): EPIC (arXiv:2410.15332, ICML 2025 poster, OpenReview qjd3ZUiHRT) explicitly introduces Position-Independent Caching (PIC), enabling KV cache reuse of a text chunk regardless of preceding prefix/position, avoiding full prefill recomputation per new context. The abstract states existing caching requires exact prefix matches (a limitation in RAG/few-shot where immutable docs sit behind varying prefixes), and EPIC's PIC enables modular reuse via AttnLink/LegoLink (selective recompute to recover accuracy) + KVSplit chunking. Reported up to 8x TTFT and 7x throughput gains with negligible accuracy loss. The claim faithfully paraphrases the paper — no overreach. Source is the primary peer-reviewed paper (ICML 2025), current (2024-2025), not marketing. Claim strength matches source strength.

### [15] EPIC's core algorithm LegoLink heals cross-context attention by targeting the 'attention sink' effect at document/chunk boundaries, recomputing only a minimal set of tokens to restore accuracy.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://openreview.net/forum?id=qjd3ZUiHRT (primary)
Quote: "The core innovation is the LegoLink algorithm, which addresses the 'attention sink' effect that occurs at document boundaries to maintain accuracy with minimal computation overhead."
Verifier evidence (high): Multiple sources (arXiv 2410.15332, OpenReview qjd3ZUiHRT, ICML 2025 poster/slides) confirm EPIC's core algorithm is LegoLink, which targets the "attention sink" effect. Because each cached chunk's position IDs start at 0, its first few tokens acquire disproportionate sink attention; when spliced at a non-zero position this is wrong. LegoLink recomputes only the first k tokens of each chunk (except the genuinely-first chunk) so those tokens "learn they are not the start" and lose sink behavior, restoring accuracy with O(kN) work instead of O(N^2) full recompute. This matches the claim's three assertions: (1) heals cross-context attention, (2) targets attention sink at chunk/document boundaries, (3) recomputes a minimal token set. Source quality is strong: authors' own paper, ICML 2025 acceptance, independent literature reviews.

### [16] EPIC implements Position-Independent Caching (PIC), enabling reuse of a chunk's KV vectors regardless of what prefix precedes it, rather than requiring exact prefix matches.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.15332 (primary)
Quote: "Position-Independent Caching (PIC) addresses this issue by enabling modular reuse of the KV vectors regardless of prefixes."
Verifier evidence (high): Claim matches primary source exactly. arxiv 2410.15332 (EPIC, ICML 2025 poster #43926) states PIC "enables modular reuse of the KV vectors regardless of prefixes," and abstract frames the problem as existing caching "requires exact prefix matches." Corroborated by independent summaries (emergentmind, themoonlight). EPIC implements PIC via AttnLink/LegoLink (static-sparsity selective recompute) and KVSplit chunking. Reported 8x TTFT / 7x throughput, accuracy drop <7%. Current (Oct 2024, ICML 2025), primary-sourced, no contradicting evidence found.

### [17] EPIC's core mechanism is the LegoLink algorithm, which heals cross-attention by mitigating the spurious 'attention sink' effect that appears at every reused document's beginning, using minimal recomputation.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.15332 (primary)
Quote: "introducing EPIC, a serving system incorporating our new LegoLink algorithm, which mitigates the inappropriate "attention sink" effect at every document beginning, to maintain accuracy with minimal computation"
Verifier evidence (high): The primary source abstract (arXiv:2410.15332) states EPIC "incorporat[es] our new LegoLink algorithm, which mitigates the inappropriate 'attention sink' effect at every document beginning, to maintain accuracy with minimal computation" — directly matching the claim. Independent summaries (Moonlight review, EmergentMind, OpenReview/ICML 2025 poster) confirm the mechanism: LegoLink dynamically recomputes a small number k of initial tokens per chunk (O(kN), k<<N) to neutralize the attention-sink effect where initial chunk tokens absorb excessive attention. The claim accurately characterizes LegoLink as the healing/recompute mechanism with minimal recomputation. Minor framing nit: EPIC's overarching contribution is Position-Independent Caching (PIC), with LegoLink as its central algorithm — but calling LegoLink the 'core mechanism' for healing cross-attention is fair and consistent with the sources. Source is the peer-reviewed primary paper (ICML 2025), quality sufficient; claim is current (2024-2025).

### [18] llama.cpp exposes a KV-cache sequence-shift API (llama_kv_cache_seq_shift) that performs RoPE-based position shifting of cached keys during context swapping, invoked when the context window fills.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/5652 (primary)
Quote: "User @ngxson reported that `llama_kv_cache_seq_shift` and `llama_kv_cache_seq_rm` functions fail when the K cache uses q4_0 quantization format. The crash occurs during context swapping—the mechanism that removes old tokens to make room for new ones when the context window fills."
Verifier evidence (high): Verified against llama.cpp source and docs. llama.cpp's KV-cache update/shift mechanism (originally llama_kv_cache_seq_shift, later renamed llama_kv_cache_seq_add) builds a computation graph that applies RoPE adjustments to the cached K tensors to reflect new relative positions without re-processing tokens — exactly the "RoPE-based position shifting of cached keys" the claim describes. It is invoked during "context shift" when the window fills: seq_add with a negative offset slides the window back to make room. Issue #5652 confirms the function's existence and its role in context swapping (the q4_0 crash occurred precisely during this shift). DeepWiki (ggml-org/llama.cpp, qualcomm/llama.cpp) corroborates: "seq_add (shift positions)... updates the RoPE frequencies of existing tokens in the cache." The only minor imprecision is the API name (renamed seq_shift→seq_add), which does not affect the substantive claim. Current: Discussion #24944 (2026) shows the mechanism is still active/maintained, with shifting hard-disabled only on M-RoPE architectures (Qwen3.5/3.6, Gemma4).

### [19] The position-shift/RoPE operation manipulates the raw K (key) tensor in the cache, and fails when that K tensor is stored quantized as q4_0 (V remains f16), crashing with assertions in ggml.c.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/5652 (primary)
Quote: "The llama_kv_cache_seq_shift or llama_kv_cache_seq_rm (or all two of them) is broken with cache type q4_0 for K."
Verifier evidence (high): Primary source llama.cpp issue #5652 states verbatim: "The llama_kv_cache_seq_shift or llama_kv_cache_seq_rm (or all two of them) is broken with cache type q4_0 for K." The reporter runs with --cache-type-k q4_0 and on context-swap/shift the program crashes with repeated "GGML_ASSERT: ggml.c:12646: false" assertion failures. Workaround given is --no-context-shift. This matches the claim on all points: the shift operation touches the raw K tensor (RoPE-based position shift), fails specifically when K is quantized q4_0 (V is f16 by default), and crashes with ggml.c assertions. The claim is not an overreach — it faithfully restates the issue. Source is the authoritative upstream repo (github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp), matching the claim's strength.


## Unverified claims (5 — verifier agents failed; neither confirmed nor refuted)
- "llama.cpp's KV cache implementation exposes a seq_add() operation that shifts cached token positions forward by a delta (RoPE re-anchoring), enabling reuse of cached K/V at a new position offset." (https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/src/llama-kv-cache.cpp, 3/3 votes errored)
- "llama.cpp provides a seq_div() operation that divides/compresses cached token positions by a divisor, the mechanism used by Self-Extend for position compression of the KV cache." (https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/src/llama-kv-cache.cpp, 3/3 votes errored)
- "When positions of cached K change (context shift), llama.cpp builds a dedicated compute graph (build_graph_shift) that re-applies rotary position embeddings to the cached K tensors, but only when the model uses RoPE." (https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/src/llama-kv-cache.cpp, 3/3 votes errored)
- "CacheBlend selects which tokens to recompute by measuring the L2 distance between newly computed and cached keys at an early check layer (typically Layer 1) and picking the top tokens with the largest deviation per a configured recomp_ratio (~15%)." (https://github.com/ForceInjection/AI-fundermentals/blob/main/09_inference_system/kv_cache/02_systems/lmcache/cache_blend.md, 3/3 votes errored)
- "CacheBlend recomputes KV only for the selected critical tokens rather than the whole context, trading minimal recompute for accurate reuse of non-prefix KV cache." (https://github.com/ForceInjection/AI-fundermentals/blob/main/09_inference_system/kv_cache/02_systems/lmcache/cache_blend.md, 3/3 votes errored)

Mention in caveats that 5 claim(s) could not be verified due to infrastructure errors.

## Instructions
1. Identify claims that say the same thing — merge them, combine their sources.
2. Group related claims into coherent findings. Each finding should directly address the research question.
3. Assign confidence per finding: high (multiple primary sources, unanimous votes), medium (secondary sources or split votes), low (single source or blog-quality).
4. Write a 3-5 sentence executive summary answering the research question.
5. Note caveats: what's uncertain, what sources were weak, what time-sensitivity applies.
6. List 2-4 open questions that emerged but weren't answered.

Structured output only.

attachment.content:
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
